review.summary: Archaeologists identify movement of Thule Inuit from Alaska through Arctic Canada into Greenland. An influential chronology places its initial broad expansion in the thirteenth century. This entry displays that model with two regional proxies; the connecting line is schematic and conveys no intermediate itinerary, single migrating party, or direction at every stage.
review.limitations: The movement is well established at broad scale; onset, duration and rate are less secure. Arctic dating faces material-age, reservoir and context problems. review.discussion: Friesen's synthesis favors a very rapid expansion; Park argues that chronological and demographic evidence permits or favors a process spanning centuries. These sources do not establish a simple extermination narrative: archaeological replacement and overlap do not by themselves demonstrate violence or the fate of individuals.

review.summary: After the US–Dakota War, a military commission sentenced 303 Dakota prisoners to death. President Abraham Lincoln authorized 39 executions; after a reprieve, US authorities hanged 38 Dakota men at Mankato on 26 December 1862. More than 1,600 Dakota people were imprisoned at Fort Snelling; many died in the winter, and the army expelled captives to Crow Creek in May 1863 after congressional legislation.
review.limitations: The 38 executions are a documented count, not the total deaths caused by the war, camp imprisonment or expulsion. MNHS estimates 130–300 deaths in the Fort Snelling camp during winter 1862–63; that estimate remains separate. The commission’s findings are not accepted as a neutral determination of guilt, and a review of every trial was not undertaken here. The memorial point covers only Mankato, not the multi-location coercive process.
review.discussion: This overlay groups execution and immediate punitive aftermath because they belong to the documented 1862–63 sequence, while preserving the distinct mechanisms and casualty measures. Lincoln’s 6 December order initially specified 19 December; the actual execution occurred on 26 December. Dakota people survived, maintained communities, and created public remembrance. No inference that all Dakota participated in the war or disappeared after expulsion is made.

Survivor families pursued compensation and preserved the event in oral accounts and visual histories; these continuities matter alongside the loss.
